chat.author: Rob Austein
chat.text: Tye protocol was designed to allow negotiaiont of what each party understands, which is why the version bump.  That does not mean that it has to take seven years to add a PDU type, just that people have to be willing to ship a version that accomplishes the purpose and leave further changes for a future version.

chat.author: Job Snijders
chat.text: RTR v0 got widely deployed, RTR v1 did not get deployed, RTR v2 is the next one to see wide scale deployment. This, among other things, means that we are for the first time venturing into an actual "protocol version negotiation" situation in the field. I really really think we need to first hear back from the field on how that all went before deciding on what the shape of v3 will be

chat.author: John Scudder
chat.text: If I understand this correctly it doesn't affect any of the protocol elements, it's implementation suggestions?

chat.author: Rob Austein
chat.text: My impression as well.  Existing implementations vary so some may already follow some of these rules.

chat.author: John Scudder
chat.text: If so I will observe we have a long tradition in this WG and its predecessors about reporting implementation experience, without turning those implementation reports into RFCs or working group documents.

chat.author: Rob Austein
chat.text: Some of this is probably historical: earliest RPKI validator used RFC 3779 implementation that tightly integrated X.509 validation with RFC 3779 validation, so we tended to verify signatures more than strictly required.  One can do better than that, at least some of what I'm seeing here looks like an attempt to do better.  Fair enough.
